players.product: High-capacity nearline HDDs (UltraSMR / EPMR / HAMR) for AI capacity-tier storage

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 FY2027 results (CFO): revenue was $4.4 billion, up 55% year over year, driven by strong exabyte growth (rendered 'expedited' in the transcript) and a favorable pricing environment; WD shipped 248 exabytes, up 22% year over year and up 8% sequentially. Cloud revenue was $3.9 billion, 88% of total revenue, up 54% year over year, driven by demand for high-capacity nearline HDDs including the initial ramp of the latest ePMR platform; Client was 7% of revenue at $320 million, up 119%; Consumer was 5% at $193 million, up 19%. Gross margin expanded to 58.1%, up 1,420 basis points year over year, with incremental year-over-year gross margin above 80%; the year-over-year growth in average price per terabyte increased to 28% versus the high teens reported in the prior quarter. Operating expenses were $391 million (approximately 9% of revenue); operating income of $2.2 billion rose 152%; operating margin 49.1%; EPS $4.64, up 161%. Free cash flow was $1.4 billion; the quarter ended with a net cash position of half a billion. CEO Irving Tan: results were 'ahead of our expectations'.
quarterly_data.figure: Revenue $4.4 billion (+55% YoY); 248 exabytes (+22% YoY, +8% QoQ); Cloud $3.9 billion (88%, +54%); gross margin 58.1% (+1,420 bps); price per terabyte +28% YoY; operating margin 49.1%; EPS $4.64 (+161%); free cash flow $1.4 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Outlook for Q2 FY2027 (CFO), in 'an environment of strong demand and favorable pricing, in all our end markets': revenue of $5.1 billion plus or minus $100 million, which at the midpoint reflects a 69% increase year over year; gross margin of 60 to 61% from the shift to higher-capacity drives and a strong pricing environment; operating expenses of $400 to $410 million, a sequential increase from expenses related to increased product qualification activities; interest and other expenses of $15 million; tax rate 17%; diluted EPS of $5.80 plus or minus $0.20 on 380 million shares. CFO: WD expects to accelerate exabyte supply growth (rendered 'expedited' in the transcript) throughout fiscal year 2027 and 2028 as it executes its technology and product transitions.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 FY2027 guide: revenue $5.1 billion +/- $100 million (+69% YoY at midpoint); gross margin 60 to 61%; opex $400 to $410 million; EPS $5.80 +/- $0.20

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR and ePMR roadmap (CEO Irving Tan): volume production of the latest ePMR platform, up to 40 terabytes, 'is off to a strong start', customer adoption is 'progressing ahead of prior transitions', and the platform is expected to be close to 30% of nearline shipments by the second quarter and 50% by the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (management in Q&A: 'the fastest transition of any EPMR platform that we've seen'). First-generation HAMR: 'on track to finish qualifications with two hyperscale customers in the first quarter of calendar year 2027', 'on schedule to begin volume shipments in the first half of calendar year 2027', and qualifications with two additional customers are expected to begin in the first half of calendar year 2027; customer feedback has been 'very positive, particularly around the failure rates'. Starting in the second half of calendar 2027 WD will begin qualification of second-generation HAMR drives at '5 terabytes per platter on a 11-disc platform'; CEO: 'we're very quickly at the top end going from a 32 terabyte drive to a 44 terabyte drive to a 55 terabyte drive'. Management also cited a roadmap, shown at the February innovation day, to drives with up to 14 platters.
quarterly_data.figure: up to 40 terabyte ePMR platform close to 30% of nearline shipments by Q2 and 50% by Q3 FY2027; first-generation HAMR qualifications with two hyperscale customers to finish Q1 CY2027, volume shipments to begin H1 CY2027; second-generation HAMR 5 terabytes per platter, 11-disc, qualification from H2 CY2027

quarterly_data.signal: Visibility and LTAs: CEO Irving Tan said that for the top seven customers 'we have good visibility up to 2030, 2031 for across all seven' and 'quarter after quarter, the demand signal actually increasing over time'; customers 'continue to extend their planning horizons into the next decade'. LTA structure (management): LTAs carry 'contractual price increases as we move into different periods'; 'some of the LTAs are expiring and new agreements are being put on place', and some exabytes are not under contracts, with 'a very strong price environment' for those; WD also gets 'better spot pricing with nearline customers who aren't on LTAs, given the tight supply environment'. LTAs have base volume and upside volume, and 'the further you go out, the less of it is covered under LTAs'.
quarterly_data.figure: good visibility up to 2030, 2031 across the top seven customers

quarterly_data.signal: Supply and demand (management): demand continues at '25% plus CAGR, as we've highlighted consistently in a very tight supply' environment, and WD remains 'committed to not investing in any incremental unit capacity', meeting growth through areal density. CEO: 'We sort of see the current quarter as being sort of the floor' for exabyte growth, accelerating through the rest of the fiscal year and into fiscal 2028; 'There hasn't been any diminishing in demand, and we don't see the gap in supply or demand that exists today perishable in the near term'. Management said its long-term nearline exabyte growth view is 'greater than 25%'; it is currently slightly below 25% 'because we're in between those two product transitions', and 'as the product transitions are getting more traction, we will exceed that 25%'. CFO: the transitions to the up to 44 terabyte ePMR platform and first- and second-generation HAMR 'will definitely accelerate our exabyte year-over-year supply growth over the next six, seven, eight quarters'; on going beyond one quarter: 'we only guide in one quarter at a time'.
quarterly_data.figure: demand 25% plus CAGR; exabyte growth 22% in Q1, seen as the floor; long-term nearline exabyte growth greater than 25%; exabyte supply growth to accelerate over the next six, seven, eight quarters

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing and margin outlook (management): average selling price per terabyte was up 28% year over year, with strength 'across the board in nearline and non-nearline', including client and consumer; one quarter earlier it was 18%; management: for 'the next three, four quarters', there's definitely further room to expand our ASP per terabyte year-over-year growth', though 'I would assume eventually that is going to slow down a little bit'. HAMR is not discounted versus ePMR: 'we price them on a dollar per terabyte basis' and 'whether we ship a hammer bit or EPMR bit, the price is the price'. CEO Irving Tan on gross margin: 'the sustainability of gross margin expansion is absolutely there', from three drivers - pricing (LTA price steps, spot pricing, client and consumer), upmix to higher-capacity drives, and more exabytes through higher areal density without the fixed cost of more units.
quarterly_data.figure: ASP per terabyte +28% YoY (18% a quarter earlier); further room to expand over the next three, four quarters

quarterly_data.signal: Cost per terabyte and memory input costs (CFO): WD is 'well on track in the long run to reduce our cost per terabyte approximately 10% year over year', but 'we use some DRAM and some NAND inside our hard disk drives' and 'the whole supply chain really operates in a very tight environment', so WD faces input cost increases it is addressing through value engineering that 'takes a little bit of time to implement and qualify'; 'in the near term, our cost per terabyte will be less than 10% down year over year'. Incremental gross margins 'continue to be very strong well above 80%'.
quarterly_data.figure: long-run cost per terabyte down approximately 10% YoY; near term less than 10% down; incremental gross margin well above 80%

quarterly_data.signal: Capex and heads / media (management): capital expenditures are expected to average 4 to 6% of revenue over a five-year period, but 'modestly above that range over the next two years', to 'invest in heads and media technology and factory automation' supporting areal density and higher-capacity drives 'without having to spend capex to add unit capacity'. HAMR heads require more cycles to produce ('a bit of throughput loss') and HAMR head wafers and media involve longer cycle times, so WD is adding head capacity, which management said does not translate into more units; the platter-count roadmap (up to 14 platters) also needs more heads per drive. WD uses 'some external head capacity' and external media in a build-and-buy approach to benchmark its components; 'what we do buy from third parties typically used in our lower capacity drives' and 'all the high-cap leading-edge platforms that we introduce are all on our own internal heads'. Management contrasted WD with 'maybe one other player in the market who is dependent on third-party supplies' and not vertically integrated, and said its response to any competitor's unit-capacity expansion stays a focus on areal density.
quarterly_data.figure: capex 4 to 6% of revenue on average over five years, modestly above that range over the next two years

quarterly_data.signal: Customer base and demand drivers: CEO Irving Tan said storage demand is growing beyond core cloud and hyperscale customers into enterprise and newer end markets 'such as NeoClouds and AI frontier labs', and management said in Q&A that demand is coming 'from the frontier AI labs, from the neocloud players, and also hybrid cloud solution OEM providers'. Management named four growth drivers - cloud growth (accelerating, with more video content and AI-enabled services), model training and reinforcement learning (where neoclouds play a part), inference and agentic AI ('tremendous amount of growth'), and physical AI - and said a slowdown in neoclouds would not be 'in any way a major hiccup'; WD prioritizes strategic neoclouds 'that we think have a very strong balance sheet'. Physical AI: 'some of our customers in Asia who are in the autonomous vehicle space are definitely looking for increased demands supply from us', robotics is 'becoming a key area', expected to spread beyond Asia over the next two to three years.

High-bandwidth drive (CEO Irving Tan): WD is expanding the role of HDDs in cloud and AI infrastructure through its high-bandwidth drive and dual pivot technology and is 'currently sampling our high-bandwidth drives with multiple customers' with positive feedback. The opportunity is 'still somewhat nascent today'; from the latter part of calendar 2027 and 2028 it could be 'a big differentiator', letting customers use HDDs for workloads such as KV cache in AI inferencing and video streaming; WD is 'working through the sort of commercial construct of how we would price that going forward'.
